articles.title: Our market study said 92% of rental businesses can't take online bookings. The real figure was 69%.
articles.excerpt: I'm building Renviq, software for small car, motorbike and boat rental businesses. We wanted a number we could stand behind: how many of these businesses can actually be booked online? So we pulled 1,…
articles.body: I'm building Renviq, software for small car, motorbike and boat rental businesses. We wanted a number we could stand behind: how many of these businesses can actually be booked online? So we pulled 1,759 rental businesses from Google Maps across five Spanish tourist areas (Mallorca, Ibiza, Málaga, Alicante, Tenerife), downloaded each homepage, and looked for a booking engine. Result: 8% bookable. 92% can't take an online booking. A beautiful headline for someone selling booking software. It was wrong. A plain download runs no JavaScript, so it misses every booking widget injected by a script, loaded in an iframe or living on a sub-page. We re-checked a stratified sample of 119 in a real browser, three passes each.

articles.body: A SQL query can run successfully and still return the wrong result. Imagine your manager asks you to find the three highest-paid employees in the IT department. articles.title: My Server Was Down for 4 Hours and I Didn't Know: A 15-Line Prometheus Alert That Finally Pings My Phone
articles.excerpt: My Server Was Down for 4 Hours and I Didn't Know: A 15-Line Prometheus Alert That Finally Pings My Phone Last month I found out about a production outage the worst way possible: a client told me. "You…
articles.body: My Server Was Down for 4 Hours and I Didn't Know: A 15-Line Prometheus Alert That Finally Pings My Phone Last month I found out about a production outage the worst way possible: a client told me. "Your API has been timing out since the night shift." I checked uptime, grabbed my phone, and realized my monitoring dashboard had shown "all healthy" the whole time. The check I'd set up was only looking at whether the process was running. The process was running. It just wasn't answering requests. That's the trap most of us fall into: we monitor the thing we know how to measure, not the thing that actually breaks. Here's the 15-line alert rule that closed that gap for me — and the mental model that made it work.

articles.title: AI Agent Swarms vs. a Single Agent: Build a Fair Coordination Benchmark
articles.excerpt: A team of four AI agents recently defeated Minecraft's Ender Dragon. In a separate experiment, a 50-agent colony tried to build a thriving civilization, then ran into resource scarcity and coordinatio…
articles.body: A team of four AI agents recently defeated Minecraft's Ender Dragon. In a separate experiment, a 50-agent colony tried to build a thriving civilization, then ran into resource scarcity and coordination overhead. Both results are interesting. Neither, by itself, proves that more agents make a better system. The comparison is useful because it exposes the real engineering question: when does parallel work outweigh coordination overhead? The four-agent run used a randomly generated world on Easy difficulty. The agents wrote 2,783 programs, died 605 times, and finished the objective in 27 hours and 14 minutes. The authors say the agents coordinated using chat and shared memory, without human-assigned roles or game logic.[2] The 50-agent colony had a different goal and setup.

articles.title: My retry budget taught me that 'just try again' is a spending decision, not a strategy
articles.excerpt: When I started exposing APIs that agents call autonomously, I kept seeing the same failure pattern: a downstream hiccup and the calling agent would fire the same request again immediately, then again,…
articles.body: When I started exposing APIs that agents call autonomously, I kept seeing the same failure pattern: a downstream hiccup and the calling agent would fire the same request again immediately, then again, then again — a tight retry loop that turned a 30-second blip into a small denial-of-service against my own service. So I implemented a retry budget. Each agent gets a bounded number of retries per endpoint per time window, with exponential backoff and jitter, plus a circuit breaker that tells callers "stop, come back later" instead of letting them burn attempts against a degraded dependency. The surprise wasn't technical — it was behavioral. Agents that received a clear Retry-After plus a remaining-budget header actually backed off gracefully. Agents that got a bare 500 just retried harder.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 29, 1991: NASA's Galileo spacecraft flies by asteroid Gaspra and snaps amazing photos while flying at 18,000 mph
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 29, 1991, the Galileo spacecraft flew by the asteroid Gaspra on its way to Jupiter. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 29, 1991, the Galileo spacecraft flew by the asteroid Gaspra on its way to Jupiter. Gaspra was the first asteroid to ever be visited by a spacecraft. Gaspra orbits near the inner edge of the asteroid belt . The Galileo spacecraft had been travelling through the asteroid belt for about two months before it reached Gaspra. Galileo was 990 miles (1,593 kilometers) away from Gaspra when it whizzed by, and it was travelling at a relative speed of about 5 miles (8 km) per second. The spacecraft took several photos of the asteroid and used an instrument called the Near-Infrared Mapping Spectrometer to study its chemical composition and other physical properties. Galileo determined that Gaspra has an irregular and elongated shape measuring about 12 miles long and 7 miles wide.

articles.title: Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman named deputy director for NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory
articles.excerpt: The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty.
articles.body: The leader of NASA's first mission around the moon in half a century is the last to announce what's next for him after retiring from active astronaut duty. All four astronauts of the Artemis II mission, which flew around the moon in April, have hung up their spacesuits and moved on to greener pastures. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), managed by Caltech, announced yesterday that former NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman will step into the role of Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of JPL, beginning Nov. 30. "Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a JPL press release .
